title: Nonconservative Forces
lead: Not every force gives back what is done against it. This section is about the forces that do not, with friction as the plain example: the work done by a nonconservative force depends on the path taken, so no potential energy can be defined for it, and what it removes from a system becomes thermal energy that cannot be fully recovered. You will see that the work done by all the nonconservative forces acting on a system is exactly the change in that system’s mechanical energy, and that writing the account this way is usually a shorter road to a distance or a speed than combining force vectors would be.
objectives: Define nonconservative forces and explain how they affect mechanical energy.
Show how the principle of conservation of energy can be applied by treating the conservative forces in terms of their potential energies and any nonconservative forces in terms of the work they do.
summary_html:
• A nonconservative force is one for which work depends on the path.
  • Friction is an example of a nonconservative force that changes mechanical energy into thermal energy.
  • Work $\kWnc$ done by a nonconservative force changes the mechanical energy of a system. In equation form, $$\kWnc = \kdKE + \kdPE$$ or, equivalently, $$\kKEi + \kPEi + \kWnc = \kKEf + \kPEf.$$
  • When both conservative and nonconservative forces act, energy conservation can be applied and used to calculate motion in terms of the known potential energies of the conservative forces and the work done by nonconservative forces, instead of finding the net work from the net force, or having to directly apply Newton’s laws.

figures.original_caption: The amount of the happy face erased depends on the path taken by the eraser between points A and B, as does the work done against friction. Less work is done and less of the face is erased for the path in (a) than for the path in (b). The force here is friction, and most of the work goes into thermal energy that subsequently leaves the system (the happy face plus the eraser). The energy expended cannot be fully recovered.

Comparison of the effects of conservative and nonconservative forces on the mechanical energy of a system. (a) A system with only conservative forces. When a rock is dropped onto a spring, its mechanical energy remains constant (neglecting air resistance) because the force in the spring is conservative. The spring can propel the rock back to its original height, where it once again has only potential energy due to gravity. (b) A system with nonconservative forces. When the same rock is dropped onto the ground, it is stopped by nonconservative forces that dissipate its mechanical energy as thermal energy, sound, and surface distortion. The rock has lost mechanical energy.

A person pushes a crate up a ramp, doing work on the crate. Friction and gravitational force (not shown) also do work on the crate; both forces oppose the person’s push. As the crate is pushed up the ramp, it gains mechanical energy, implying that the work done by the person is greater than the work done by friction.
The baseball player slides to a stop in a distance d. In the process, friction removes the player’s kinetic energy by doing an amount of work fd equal to the initial kinetic energy.

exercises.prompt: You are in a room in a basement with a smooth concrete floor (friction force equals 40 N) and a nice rug (friction force equals 55 N) that is 3 m by 4 m. However, you have to push a very heavy box from one corner of the rug to the opposite corner of the rug. Will you do more work against friction going around the floor or across the rug, and how much extra?

options: Across the rug is 275 J extra
Around the floor is 5 J extra
Across the rug is 5 J extra
Around the floor is 280 J extra
answer.hint: The rug is 3 m by 4 m, so the diagonal across it is 5 m, while going round two of its edges on the concrete is 7 m. Work out the friction force times the distance for each route and compare the two.

exercises.prompt: In the Appalachians, along the interstate, there are ramps of loose gravel for semis that have had their brakes fail to drive into to stop. Design an experiment to measure how effective this would be.

answer.solution: Build the ramp to scale on a bench and send a loaded cart into it, since what you want to measure is the distance a vehicle of known mass and known speed travels before the gravel has taken all of its kinetic energy. Lay a tray of loose gravel at the end of a level run, release the cart from a measured height on a track so that you know the speed it arrives with, and measure the distance $\kd$ it travels into the gravel before it stops. The energy account is $\tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvi}^2 = \kff\kd + m\kg\kh$, where $\kh$ is the height the cart rises if the ramp is tilted upward, so the average retarding force follows from the distance you measured. Repeat with the cart released from several heights and plot the stopping distance against the square of the arrival speed: a straight line says the retarding force is constant, and its slope gives you that force. Then vary what the ramp is made of, deep gravel against shallow gravel against bare board, and vary the load on the cart, and you can say which ramp stops a given vehicle in the shortest distance and how long the ramp would have to be for a semi arriving at highway speed.

exercises.prompt: A 60.0-kg skier with an initial speed of 12.0 m/s coasts up a 2.50-m-high rise as shown in the figure at the end of the section. Find her final speed at the top, given that the coefficient of friction between her skis and the snow is 0.0800. (Hint: Find the distance traveled up the incline assuming a straight-line path as shown in the figure.)

answer.hint: Her kinetic energy at the bottom has to pay both for the height she gains and for the work friction does along the slope. Take her path up the rise as a straight line, so that the distance is the height divided by $\sin 35^\circ$, and the friction force is the coefficient times the component of her weight perpendicular to the slope.
